meta.attribution: Adapted from 'Shop 'til you(r profits) drop' (SaveRite), Fuqua Casebook 2019-2020, pp. 33-41. Internal test fixture and demo fallback only — not for redistribution.

prompt.spoken: Our client is SaveRite, a large national grocery retailer operating only physical stores. New leadership is under pressure to improve profits, which have been flat for three years despite growing revenue. They've asked us to identify the source of the plateau and develop a plan to increase profitability. How would you approach this?
prompt.constraint: Client wants answers fast — new leadership expects a direction, not a study.

clarifying_ledger.answer: SaveRite operates national grocery chains, physical retail locations only — no online business.
Competitors are NOT experiencing similar profitability declines. No new players have entered the market.
No information at this time on which products drive the profitability problem — worth investigating.
Simple model: buys food from suppliers, sells to customers.
Revenue has actually been growing steadily — the problem is that profit hasn't followed.

ledger_miss_policy: live_fetch_not_applicable_for_fixture; interviewer improvises a neutral 'we don't have that information, but good question' consistent with the ledger

expected_buckets: Profitability broken into Revenue and Costs (the core P = R - C tree)
Revenue: product mix carried, foot traffic / customer base, expansion opportunities
Costs: fixed (capex, rent for physical footprint) vs variable (COGS through the supply chain, labor)
acceptable_buckets: Overall market / competitive dynamics bucket — fine to include, but the case does not reward exploring it
buckets_to_avoid_dwelling_on: Competition and market dynamics — explicitly not important for this case (competitors are healthy, no new entrants)
great_candidate_signals: Hypothesis-driven: suspects a cost problem early since revenue is growing while profit is flat
Tailors the tree to grocery retail specifics rather than reciting a generic framework

quant_module.setup_spoken: So you mentioned you'd want to look at the client's financials — I have SaveRite's income statement for the last three years, 2012 through 2014. I'll read the figures out; feel free to jot these down. Revenue: 360, 378, then 397 million dollars. Cost of goods sold: 50, 60, then 72 million. Wages: 95, 100, 105 million. Corporate SG&A: 10, 10.5, 11 million. And overhead: 40, 42, 44 million. Take a moment with those numbers — then tell me what stands out to you, and what it means for why profits have been flat.
quant_module.expected_setup: Compute or eyeball growth rates per line; EBITDA works out flat (~165M all three years).

worked_solution.takeaway_basic: Revenue grows steadily but COGS grows ~4x faster than everything else, eating the gains — that's why profit is flat.
worked_solution.takeaway_second_order: COGS at 20% YoY against 5% everywhere else means the problem is isolated to cost of goods — the next question is WHICH goods.

followup_data_drop.trigger: Candidate asks what's inside COGS / which categories or cost components drive it
followup_data_drop.spoken: Good question. Within COGS we track four categories — fresh produce, dairy, alcohol, and dry commodities like flour and sugar — each split into direct labor, shipping, and supplier purchase price. Across three years, every component grew steadily... except one: the purchase price SaveRite pays suppliers for dry commodities, which went from 9 to 17 to 22 million.
followup_data_drop.takeaway: The entire COGS blowout localizes to supplier purchase price in dry commodities — SaveRite is being overcharged in exactly one category.

layers: Layer 1 (from verbal financials): flat profit is a COGS problem, not a revenue problem.
Layer 2 (from follow-up data drop): within COGS, it's specifically supplier purchase price for dry commodities.

kicker.trigger: Candidate asks why competitors aren't affected despite sharing the same suppliers
kicker.spoken: Sharp question. It turns out every major competitor now carries mostly PRIVATE-BRAND dry commodities — their own labels — while SaveRite still carries almost entirely national brands.
kicker.insight: Competitors escaped the supplier price squeeze by moving dry commodities to private brand; SaveRite's exposure is a portfolio choice, not bad luck.

hidden_insight.scoring: unprompted discovery of layer 2 and asking the competitor question = top marks on Insight & Drive; needing the hint prompts = middle; never localizing beyond 'costs are up' = miss

brainstorm_module.prompt_spoken: Before you wrap up — what are some ways SaveRite could reduce cost of goods sold in dry commodities?
sample_answers: Reduce order quantities to cut holding and inventory costs
Develop relationships with new, cheaper suppliers
Build out a private-brand product line (the case's intended headline answer)
brainstorm_module.note: Structure of the brainstorm matters more than hitting every item; private brand should be teased out via the kicker if not raised

recommendation_key.expected_recommendation: Shift SaveRite's dry-commodities assortment toward private brand to escape supplier overcharging, while renegotiating national-brand contracts in parallel.
recommendation_key.supporting_logic: Profit is flat solely because dry-commodities purchase price is growing ~40%+ YoY; competitors neutralized the same pressure via private brand.
risks: Customer perception: private brands may read as lower quality (though category may be perception-insensitive for flour/sugar staples)
Execution: sourcing/manufacturing private brand requires capabilities SaveRite may lack
Supplier retaliation on other categories during the transition
mitigations: Pilot private brand in a subset of stores/SKUs before chain-wide rollout
Run customer willingness-to-pay research on dry commodities specifically
Stagger contract renegotiations so no supplier relationship breaks all at once
next_steps: Size the margin uplift of a private-brand shift (target the ~13M excess vs trend in dry-commodities purchase price)
Define pilot store cohort and success metrics
